title: Add iter_ranges and format_ranges for page-range specs
description: Adds two functions to `more_itertools/more.py` for the range specs that print dialogs and command-line flags accept, such as `1-3, 7, 10-12`. `iter_ranges(spec, limit=10_000)` returns an iterator over the numbers a spec names: parts are separated by commas, whitespace around a part is ignored and empty parts are skipped, and each part is a number or two numbers joined by `-` (both ends included), written with the ASCII digits 0 to 9 only. Numbers come out in the order the spec names them, each one once. Specs usually come from users, so the whole spec is checked when `iter_ranges` is called and a bad spec raises ValueError right there, before any number is produced. A spec is bad if a part is not a number or range, if a range ends below its start (`3-3` is fine), or if its parts name more than `limit` numbers in total, counting a number again each time a part names it. `format_ranges(iterable)` goes the other way: it takes non-negative integers in any order, with repeats, and writes runs of three or more consecutive integers as `start-end` and the others one by one, in increasing order (`[3, 1, 2, 7, 9, 10]` gives `1-3,7,9,10`). It accepts only integers (anything with `__index__`): a negative one raises ValueError, and a float, string or other object raises TypeError. Includes type stubs and tests.

defects.summary: The part pattern uses \d, which matches every Unicode decimal digit, so specs written in other scripts' digits or full-width digits are accepted instead of rejected.
The limit is compared with the size of one part instead of the running total, so a user can name any amount of numbers by splitting them over several parts.
The parts are no longer collected before numbers are produced, so a bad spec is only noticed while iterating, after the numbers before it were already handed out.
Values are converted with int(), so strings and floats are silently accepted (and floats truncated) instead of raising TypeError.
A range whose end equals its start, such as 3-3, is rejected as ending before it starts.
Runs of two consecutive integers are written as start-end, although only runs of three or more should be.

ceiling.summary: The limit is converted with int() instead of operator.index like format_ranges' values, so a float limit is silently truncated and a string limit such as '10' is accepted instead of raising TypeError.

decoys.why: The 10,000 cap is the documented default, and a spec naming exactly limit numbers is allowed; only more raises.
Skipping empty parts (as in 1,,2 or a trailing comma) is the documented behaviour.
